lead.topic: Striking EEB paper: fungal hybridization and cryptic genomic diversity
lead.headline: A fungal isolate carries genomes from two species
lead.deck: Reanalysis of two clinical fungal genomes reveals an interspecies hybrid and an unsampled parental lineage.
paragraphs: A newly described fungal pathogen may be hiding two evolutionary histories inside one cell. Álvaro Redondo-Río and Toni Gabaldón revisited published genome assemblies from two clinical isolates labeled Rhodosporidiobolus fluvialis. One isolate had roughly twice the genome size of the other. That could suggest an ordinary diploid, but its two chromosome sets were much more different than expected for copies from the same species. The authors compared sequence matches, read coverage and phylogenetic trees, evolutionary family trees built from shared genes. Their analyses support an allodiploid: a hybrid carrying one chromosome set from each of two different species.

One subgenome resembled R. fluvialis, although its distance from the other clinical isolate raised questions about species boundaries. The second matched no sampled species closely, pointing to a missing parent in public genome databases. The investigators found little evidence of recombination between the subgenomes, and one region of the first subgenome hinted at an older episode of introgression, the movement of DNA across species boundaries. This is a reinterpretation of existing sequence data, not a demonstration that hybridization caused the fungus to infect people or resist drugs. It also exposes a practical problem: pathogen names based on a few marker sequences can conceal deeply divergent genomes.
lead.push: Sequence more isolates from clinical and environmental collections, especially potential relatives of the unsampled parental lineage. Then test whether the two subgenomes differ in expression, drug susceptibility or host interaction. A hybrid genome may explain unusual phenotypes, but only comparisons with nonhybrid relatives and experiments can separate that hypothesis from lineage-specific effects.

people.name: Álvaro Redondo-Río
people.bio: Álvaro Redondo-Río is a bioinformatician affiliated with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center and IRB Barcelona. A university faculty profile also lists him as a collaborating professor at Universitat Internacional de Catalunya. He trained in biochemistry at the University of Córdoba and earned a master's degree in bioinformatics at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid. His research includes fungal hybrid genomes.

people.name: Toni Gabaldón
people.bio: Toni Gabaldón is an ICREA Research Professor leading comparative genomics at IRB Barcelona and the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. After a PhD in medical sciences at Radboud University Nijmegen, he held an EMBO postdoctoral fellowship in Valencia and led a group at the Centre for Genomic Regulation. His research links genome evolution with the emergence and adaptation of fungal pathogens.

slot2.headline: Inversions can protect locally adapted genes
slot2.body: Why do chromosome inversions sometimes spread even when they initially seem disruptive? Kirkpatrick and Barton modeled two populations exchanging migrants while adapting to different environments. An inversion flips a chromosome segment and suppresses recombination in carriers with different arrangements. Their analysis showed that an inversion capturing several locally beneficial alleles can be favored because it keeps those alleles together, even without epistasis, where gene combinations have nonadditive effects. The model helped establish recombination suppression as a route to local adaptation and reproductive divergence. Later studies explored this mechanism in natural inversion systems, and a 2018 correction amended one mathematical expression.

slot3.headline: A new algorithm reveals planets hidden in starlight
slot3.cite: Ferrer-Chavez R et al. Nature (published online 4 Nov 2026). Original paper.
slot3.body: Stars overwhelm the faint light from their planets, making direct imaging difficult even for the James Webb Space Telescope. Researchers introduced FLIP, a method that builds a physical model of a telescope's starlight pattern and tunes it with machine learning before subtracting the glare. Applied to existing Webb images, it recovered a previously known giant planet, 51 Eridani b, at a wavelength where standard processing had missed it. In the tested images, sensitivity improved by factors of roughly two to fifteen. This is a better way to see faint companions, not the discovery of a new planet or proof that Earth-like worlds can already be imaged.
